justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable but modestly upward-drifting price path. For the 1-day horizon, I anchored near the prevailing market level with only a small drift adjustment, assuming no major overnight catalysts would materially shift sentiment. For the 1-week estimate, I applied a slightly larger drift to account for the natural tendency of markets to trend, while acknowledging that a week provides enough time for modest fundamental developments to nudge prices higher. For the 1-month estimate, the drift assumption compounds further, pushing the point estimate to around 1095, though I want to be clear this reflects a baseline continuation scenario rather than a strong directional conviction.

The confidence interval widths widen progressively across horizons for straightforward reasons rooted in uncertainty accumulation. Over one day, realized volatility tends to be contained, so the 90% interval spans roughly 60 points. Over a week, intraday noise compounds and macro data releases introduce additional variance, widening the band to about 110 points. Over a month, the full range of possibilities — earnings cycles, central bank communications, geopolitical developments, and shifting risk appetite — expands the plausible outcomes considerably, producing a roughly 230-point interval. These widths were calibrated loosely against typical historical volatility at each time horizon.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside these stated ranges. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharper-than-anticipated inflation reading or a sudden tightening in financial conditions — could trigger a risk-off move that breaks below the lower bounds fairly quickly. A geopolitical shock or liquidity event, while difficult to assign precise probabilities to, represents a tail risk capable of producing moves far exceeding a normal volatility assumption.

On the upside, a surprisingly dovish policy signal from a major central bank, or a strong batch of economic data suggesting a soft landing is firmly in place, could drive prices meaningfully above my upper bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon where sentiment has more room to shift. I would also note that my intervals assume relatively normal market functioning; in periods of thin liquidity or forced positioning, moves can overshoot in either direction by amounts that make even 90% confidence intervals look narrow in hindsight.
